title: Writing and balancing chemical equations
blurb: Count atoms in any formula, write equations from words and balance them with coefficients, never subscripts.
question: A study guide shows C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O and asks for the coefficient of O₂ once the equation is balanced in lowest whole numbers. Where do you start, and what must you never change?

teach.body: Formally, a chemical equation shows reactants (left) turning into products (right), with formulas, coefficients and states: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. In plain English: it is a recipe card. Subscripts tell you the atoms in one formula (H₂O = 2 H, 1 O). Coefficients tell you how many formulas (3 H₂O = 6 H, 3 O). A subscript after parentheses multiplies everything inside.

head: Written
Atoms counted
teach.caption: Atoms = coefficient × subscript. With parentheses, multiply the outside subscript by every atom inside, then by the coefficient.

teach.h: Conservation of mass: balance with coefficients
teach.body: The law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier): atoms are rearranged in a reaction, not created or destroyed, so each kind of atom appears in equal numbers on both sides and the total mass stays the same. Balance an equation by changing coefficients only. Never change a subscript: that turns the substance into something else (H₂O into H₂O₂, hydrogen peroxide).

teach.caption: The number of molecules can differ on the two sides (2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O: 3 on the left, 2 on the right). Atom counts cannot.

steps.label: Carbon
steps.sub: 3 C on the left: write 3 CO₂

steps.label: Hydrogen
steps.sub: 8 H on the left: write 4 H₂O

teach.caption: Balance atoms that appear in one formula on each side first. Leave free elements such as O₂ for last.

items: Write correct formulas first. Diatomic elements: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂.
Count every kind of atom on each side, distributing coefficients over parentheses.
Add coefficients for one element at a time, saving H, O and free elements for last.
If you need half a molecule (3.5 O₂), double every coefficient.
Reduce to the lowest whole-number ratio and check every element again.

root.label: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide

children.label: Mg + O₂ → MgO
children.sub: Oxygen gas is diatomic; MgO from Mg²⁺ and O²⁻

children.label: Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO
children.sub: 2 O on each side; now 2 Mg on the right

teach.caption: Fix the formulas before you balance. Writing MgO₂ to match the oxygen would be changing a subscript.

teach.body: Aaliyah, a radiography applicant in a prerequisite lab, heats 50.0 g of limestone in an open dish: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. The solid left weighs 28.0 g, and she worries that mass was destroyed. It was not: CO₂ gas left the dish. Mass of CO₂ = 50.0 − 28.0 = 22.0 g. In a sealed container the total would have stayed 50.0 g.

teach.h: Check a balanced equation: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O
teach.caption: An item may ask for one coefficient or for the sum: a coefficient of 1 is not written but still counts in a sum.

teach.text: Never balance by changing subscripts. Distribute the coefficient over parentheses: 2 Ca(OH)₂ has 4 O, not 2. Leave no fractions and reduce to lowest terms (4 H₂ + 2 O₂ → 4 H₂O is not finished). And a gas escaping from an open container carries mass away: mass is not destroyed.

items: Subscripts count atoms in one formula; coefficients count formulas. 2 Ca(OH)₂ = 2 Ca, 4 O, 4 H.
Conservation of mass: the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.
Balance with coefficients only; changing a subscript changes the substance.
Balance elements found in one formula first; leave H, O and free elements for last.
Finish in the lowest whole-number ratio, and count a coefficient of 1 when summing.

summary: You can now count atoms in any formula, write a balanced equation from a word description and balance equations using coefficients only. You can also use conservation of mass to explain why a reaction's total mass stays the same, even when a gas escapes.

A.q: How many oxygen atoms are represented by 2 Ca(OH)₂?
A.why: Each Ca(OH)₂ has 2 O (the subscript 2 multiplies OH). Two formula units give 2 × 2 = 4 O.

whyNot.0: 2 counts the oxygen in only one Ca(OH)₂ and ignores the coefficient.
whyNot.1: 8 multiplies by an extra 2; the count is coefficient 2 × subscript 2 = 4.
whyNot.2: 10 is the total of all atoms (2 Ca + 4 O + 4 H), not just oxygen.

A.q: When balancing a chemical equation, which numbers may be changed?
options: The coefficients in front of formulas
The charges on any ions present
A.why: Coefficients set how many formula units take part, so they are the only numbers changed when balancing.

whyNot.0: Changing a subscript changes the identity of the substance.
whyNot.2: State symbols show physical states; they do not affect the atom count.
whyNot.3: Ion charges are fixed by the elements; changing them would describe different ions.

A.q: Which coefficients balance N₂ + __ H₂ → __ NH₃?

whyNot.0: With 1 NH₃ the right has 1 N, but the left has 2.
whyNot.1: 2 H₂ gives 4 H, while 3 NH₃ gives 9 H and 3 N.
whyNot.3: 3 NH₃ gives 3 N, but the left has only 2 N.

B.q: A student heats 5.0 g of magnesium ribbon in an open dish. The white powder left weighs more than 5.0 g. What is the best explanation?
options: It combined with oxygen from air
The heat converted into extra mass
Its atoms each gained extra neutrons
Ash from the dish was added to it
B.why: Magnesium combines with oxygen from the air (2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO). The product's mass includes that oxygen, so mass is conserved overall.

whyNot.1: Heat does not create measurable mass; mass is conserved in chemical reactions.
whyNot.2: Chemical reactions involve electrons only; nuclei and neutrons are unchanged.
whyNot.3: The dish does not react; the extra mass is the oxygen that combined with the metal.

B.why: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ has 1 Ca, 1 C and 3 O on each side.

whyNot.0: The left has 2 O and the right has 1; it needs 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
whyNot.1: The right has 4 O but the left has 2; it needs 2 O₂.
whyNot.2: The left has 4 H and 4 O; the right has 2 H and 3 O. It needs 2 H₂O.

B.q: Solid aluminum reacts with oxygen gas to form aluminum oxide, Al₂O₃. Which equation is balanced?
B.why: 6 O atoms allow whole numbers of both O₂ and Al₂O₃: 3 O₂ → 2 Al₂O₃, which holds 4 Al. Check: Al 4 = 4, O 6 = 6.

whyNot.0: The left has 2 O and the right has 3, so oxygen is not balanced.
whyNot.2: O₃ and AlO₃ change formulas: oxygen gas is O₂ and aluminum oxide is Al₂O₃.
whyNot.3: Oxygen gas is diatomic; it must be written O₂, not single O atoms.

C.q: To balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, a student rewrites it as H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂. What is wrong with this?
options: It is acceptable, since the atoms now match
Changing a subscript changed the product
A coefficient of 2 should go in front of O₂
Hydrogen gas should be written as single H
C.why: Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ makes hydrogen peroxide, a different substance. Balance with coefficients: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.

whyNot.0: The atoms match, but the product is now the wrong substance; subscripts must not change.
whyNot.2: 2 O₂ would give 4 O on the left; the fix is a 2 before H₂ and before H₂O.
whyNot.3: Hydrogen is diatomic and is correctly written H₂.

C.q: When C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O is balanced in lowest whole numbers, what is the coefficient of O₂?
C.why: 2 C₂H₆ gives 4 CO₂ and 6 H₂O. Oxygen on the right = 4 × 2 + 6 = 14 atoms = 7 O₂: 2 C₂H₆ + 7 O₂ → 4 CO₂ + 6 H₂O.

whyNot.1: 3.5 O₂ balances one C₂H₆, but coefficients must be whole numbers, so every coefficient doubles.
whyNot.2: 14 is the number of oxygen atoms, not O₂ molecules.
whyNot.3: 5 is the coefficient for propane (C₃H₈); ethane needs 7 once doubled.

C.q: In the balanced equation C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O, how many oxygen atoms are on each side?

whyNot.0: 12 counts only the O₂ molecules on the left and misses glucose's 6 oxygens.
whyNot.1: 6 counts only the oxygen in one glucose molecule.
whyNot.3: 24 double-counts; each side totals 18 oxygen atoms.

reteach.title: Building with snap blocks
reteach.question: Imagine building toy cars from a bin of snap blocks. What does a balanced equation have in common with taking cars apart and building trucks from the same pieces?

blocks.body: Each car is a formula: its design (2 red, 1 blue) is the subscripts. How many cars you build is the coefficient. Taking cars apart to build trucks never adds or loses a block, so the block count before equals the count after: conservation of mass. To use up the blocks exactly, you build more or fewer trucks (change coefficients). Redesigning the truck (changing subscripts) means you are building a different toy.

rows.label: To make it come out even

blocks.text: If you change the design of a model to make the count work, you have built a different toy. In chemistry, that is changing a subscript, and it changes the substance.

explain.body: Subscripts count atoms within one formula; a subscript after parentheses multiplies everything inside. Coefficients multiply the whole formula. Total atoms = coefficient × subscript.

test.q: How many hydrogen atoms are represented by 3 H₂O?
test.why: Each H₂O has 2 H; 3 molecules have 3 × 2 = 6 H.

whyNot.1: 2 is the hydrogen count in one molecule and ignores the coefficient.
whyNot.2: 3 is the number of molecules, not the number of hydrogen atoms.
whyNot.3: 5 adds the coefficient and subscript; they must be multiplied.

explain.body: Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed. In a closed container the total mass before and after a reaction is the same. In an open one, an escaping gas carries mass away, but that mass still exists.

items.label: CaCO₃ heated in an open dish

test.q: In a sealed flask, 12.0 g of reactants react completely and form a gas that stays in the flask. What is the total mass of the products?
test.why: In a closed system mass is conserved: the products have the same total mass as the reactants, 12.0 g.

whyNot.0: No mass leaves a sealed flask; the gas is still counted.
whyNot.3: Gases have mass; the gas carries part of the 12.0 g.

explain.body: To balance, change only the coefficients. A subscript is part of the substance's identity: H₂O is water, H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide.

test.q: Which change correctly balances H₂ + Cl₂ → HCl?
options: Write Cl in place of Cl₂
test.why: 2 HCl gives 2 H and 2 Cl, matching H₂ and Cl₂: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl.

whyNot.0: H₂Cl₂ changes subscripts, which changes the substance.
whyNot.2: Chlorine gas is diatomic and must be written Cl₂.
whyNot.3: 2 H₂ puts 4 H on the left against 1 on the right, so hydrogen is still unbalanced.

explain.body: A finished equation uses whole-number coefficients in the lowest ratio. If you need half an O₂, double everything. If every coefficient shares a factor, divide it out.

test.q: A student writes 4 H₂ + 2 O₂ → 4 H₂O. What should be done to finish it?
options: Leave it; the atoms already match
test.why: The atoms balance, but 4, 2 and 4 share a factor of 2. The lowest whole-number form is 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.

whyNot.0: The atom counts match, but the coefficients are not in the lowest ratio.
whyNot.2: Changing the formula of the product changes the substance.
whyNot.3: Doubling moves further from the lowest ratio.
